tldr: For humanoid whole-body planning in confined spaces, this work introduces a rigid-body volume self-collision avoidance guide using differentiable geometry rather than infinitesimal point approximations, achieving whole-body trajectory generation and robust reinforcement learning tracking control in severe spaces where standard baselines fail.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed sequential planning pipeline. From coarse frame planning to avoid environmental collisions (Stage 1), to self-collision avoidance refinement using proxy geometry (Stage 2), and full-order whole-body trajectory optimization considering full dynamics and detailed collision geometry (Stage 3), a robust residual reinforcement learning policy executes online tracking.
overview:
When humanoids navigate extremely tight spaces (confined spaces) such as disaster sites, a slight deviation in posture causes severe collisions with the environment or their own body, leading to loss of balance. Conventional trajectory optimization (TO) often relies on oversimplified point-mass or spline-based models, or softens collision bounds with penalties, which causes severe local minima (getting stuck) in restricted environments and fails to find feasible trajectories. In addition, unnatural, extreme postures in confined spaces lack real-world motion capture data, making imitation learning hard to apply.

To address this, the authors propose a three-stage whole-body planning (WBP) framework that searches for kinematic paths directly over kinematically reachable rigid-body volumes and incorporates differentiable collision detection. First, it generates workspace paths that avoid environmental collisions, and then integrates geometric gradients of self-collision avoidance (SCA) considering proxy rigid-body volumes like capsules and spheres to produce high-quality motion seeds (guides). Passing these seeds as guides into a two-pass sequential quadratic programming (SQP) formulation that solves the full-order dynamics consistently synthesizes feasible joint torque and contact force profiles through the maze of the search space.

For validation, experiments were conducted on a 27-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid model across three benchmark testbeds exceeding NIST emergency response standards, including restricted confinement ratios of $C_r < 1.5$. While standard spline-guided baselines fail to find solutions, the proposed framework reliably generates whole-body trajectories across 12-to-18-second tasks, and a residual reinforcement learning policy trained on these references navigates the testbeds with an over 95% success rate under physical simulation disturbances and model errors.
contributions: Developed a geometry-informed kinematic reference generation method extending point-based convex relaxation planning to rigid-body volume representations, automatically discovering diverse locomotion posture seeds using differentiable geometry.

Constructed an optimization pipeline that uses kinematically consistent references as guides and applies a two-pass sequential quadratic program to evade local minima in confined spaces, generating whole-body trajectories that satisfy full-order dynamics.

Built and validated a residual reinforcement learning policy utilizing the generated whole-body trajectories as references, achieving an over 95% tracking success rate under extensive domain randomization and external perturbations.

Demonstrated 12-to-18-second long-horizon multi-contact motions on the Unitree G1 model in confined spaces exceeding NIST disaster response standards (confinement ratio $C_r < 1.5$), where conventional baselines completely fail.

sections.heading: Why is whole-body locomotion in confined spaces so challenging for humanoids?
sections.summary: While humanoid locomotion capabilities have matured, free space in confined environments degrades into non-convex, narrow manifolds, where choices of foot/hand placements and postures quickly hit dead ends. Because traditional large-scale trajectory optimization struggles with local minima from simplifications and imitation learning lacks real motion data, this paper proposes a novel whole-body planning framework using geometric seeds informed by rigid-body volumes.
sections.details:
In recent years, legged locomotion performance has rapidly matured for bipedal walking in structured environments and stepping over large obstacles. However, entering extreme confined environments, such as rubble at disaster sites or narrow passageways, presents a completely different challenge.

The fundamental difficulty is that the collision-free configuration space collapses into an extremely narrow, intricate, non-convex manifold. A slight deviation in posture causes environmental collisions and falls, and acting purely greedily on immediate contact points leads to dead ends within a few steps due to joint limits or torque exhaustion. Long-horizon whole-body planning is therefore essential.

Yet, effective tools to address this have been lacking. While learning-based and imitation learning approaches are powerful, motion capture (MoCap) data of the unnatural, extreme joint configurations that humans adopt in tight spaces is practically unavailable. Meanwhile, traditional trajectory optimization (TO) has historically neglected strict link-to-link and environment collision checks to reduce solve times, or relied on overly simplified models such as point masses and bounding boxes. Consequently, in confined spaces, optimization gets trapped in severe local minima and cannot find feasible solutions on its own.

To overcome this, the authors elevated point-mass convex relaxation planning into 3D rigid-body volumes and embedded differentiable collision detection directly into the geometric search. Providing a path toward generating diverse, dynamically consistent whole-body trajectories without manual initial guesses is the starting point of this work.

sections.heading: Limitations of optimization, imitation learning, and RL, and where this approach fits
sections.summary: Multi-contact locomotion planning has typically been tackled via optimization-based, imitation learning, or end-to-end RL approaches. However, reduced-order models cannot handle tight collisions, full-order optimization depends heavily on initialization, and learning methods suffer from data scarcity or reward exploration hurdles. This method bridges these gaps by using differentiable rigid-body geometric guides to steer the optimization space, which in turn accelerates RL.
sections.details:
Multi-contact planning, which involves establishing and breaking contacts with the environment to reach a goal, generally falls into three paradigms:

- Optimization-based methods: Typically adopt a structure where contact phases are determined prior to solving the motion. Methods using reduced-order models (ROMs) like center-of-mass abstractions are fast, but they ignore individual link collisions and cannot be applied in confined spaces. Conversely, whole-body TO considering full multi-body dynamics can model geometry faithfully; however, soft collision penalties leave residual penetrations, while hard constraints trap the optimization solver in local minima, presenting a fundamental dilemma.

- Imitation learning methods: Retargeting human MoCap data to reproduce acrobatic motions has been popular. However, it is practically impossible to collect high-quality reference datasets of extreme folded joint configurations for passing through tight spaces that respect the robot's torque and range-of-motion constraints.

- End-to-end deep reinforcement learning (RL): Policies directly mapping sensor inputs to motor commands have achieved great success on rough terrain. Nevertheless, trying to learn tasks such as slipping through narrow gaps while avoiding self- and environmental collisions from scratch via reward exploration alone leads to abysmal sample efficiency, trapping the policy in local minima or dynamic instability.

This work positions itself to bridge the weaknesses of these three avenues. By utilizing differentiable collision detection over reachable rigid-body volumes, it rapidly synthesizes geometric guides to seed full-order whole-body TO, discovering high-quality dynamically feasible trajectories. These trajectories then serve as references for residual reinforcement learning, enabling efficient training of a robust online execution controller.

sections.heading: Mathematical formulation and modular decomposition of the optimization problem
sections.summary: Multi-contact whole-body planning is an extremely challenging non-convex optimization combining continuous states/inputs with discrete contact sequence choices. This study decouples the problem by assuming the contact sequence is pre-specified, formulating it as a continuous optimization problem that satisfies dynamics, torque bounds, friction cones, and non-convex self- and environmental collision bounds within each contact phase.
sections.details:
The multi-contact locomotion problem for a legged robot can be formulated as a large-scale optimization problem that simultaneously determines the state $x(t)$, control inputs (joint torques) $u(t)$, contact phase switching times $t_i$, and total number of phases $n_{\mathrm{ph}}$.

However, solving this formulation directly is computationally intractable. In addition to the high-dimensional state space, there is a combinatorial explosion in deciding which foot or hand to place where and in what order, compounded by the strong non-convexity of geometric obstacle and self-collision constraints. Therefore, this work adopts an approach that decouples contact sequence selection from whole-body motion synthesis.

Because contact sequences can be discovered using existing tree searches or heuristics, this paper assumes an accessible sequence of contact phases $\{c_i\}_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{ph}}}$ and phase durations $T_i$ are provided in advance. This sharpens the focus onto how to discover continuous joint and torque trajectories that navigate tight gaps given the contact sequence.

In the discretized formulation, at each knot point within a contact phase, the solver must satisfy the robot's discrete multi-body dynamics, joint position and velocity limits $\mathcal{X}_{\lim}$, torque limits $\mathcal{U}$, and friction cone constraints $\mathcal{K}_i$ preventing slip at foot and hand contacts. Most challenging are the self-collision avoidance set $\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{sca}}$ and environmental collision-free set $\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{cfree}}$. In confined spaces, these feasible sets contract drastically, making it paramount to guide the solver into their basin of attraction.

sections.heading: A three-stage optimization framework paired with residual reinforcement learning tracking
sections.summary: The proposed architecture comprises three planning stages and a tracking controller. Given workspace paths avoiding environmental collisions (Stage 1), differentiable collision detection incorporates self-collision avoidance using simplified proxy geometry (Stage 2). Using this path as a guide, a two-pass trajectory optimizer resolves the full-order dynamics (Stage 3). The resulting plan is tracked robustly under disturbances via a residual reinforcement learning policy.
sections.details:
The core pipeline consists of three sequential planning stages of increasing model fidelity and computational complexity, followed by a learning-based tracking policy for execution:

- Stage 1 (Environment-Collision-Free Kinematic Planning): Decomposes the environment into convex polyhedral regions (e.g., IRIS regions) and parameterizes torso, foot, and hand task-space frame trajectories as Bézier curves. It solves a second-order cone program (SOCP) with a logarithmic penalty to constrain link length changes, yielding smooth, kinematic paths free from environmental collisions.

- Stage 2 (Volume-Informed Self-Collision Avoidance Refinement): This is the key insight. It assigns rigid-body 'volumes' to the Stage 1 paths. The torso is modeled as a capsule and the hands, knees, and ankles as spheres (proxy geometry), formulating the minimum distance between two shapes as an SOCP scale factor $\alpha$. Here, $\alpha > 1$ indicates collision-free space, while $\alpha \le 1$ denotes collision. By applying the Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) to the KKT conditions, the collision gradient with respect to the Bézier control points $\frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial \beta}$ is computed analytically. This efficiently pushes Bézier curves apart to prevent link volumes from colliding, rather than relying on point-based checks.

- Stage 3 (Full-Order Whole-Body Trajectory Optimization): Uses the smooth, self- and environmental-collision-avoiding paths from Stage 2 as tracking costs while solving the full humanoid rigid-body dynamics. It employs a 'two-pass strategy.' The first pass removes strict hard collision constraints to reconcile nonlinear dynamics and torque limits into an initial coarse plan. The second pass initializes from this plan and enforces hard signed distance field (SDF) constraints using detailed joint-level collision shapes (Fig. F3(b)), solved strictly via sequential quadratic programming (SQP). This phased approach dramatically prevents the solver from getting stuck in local minima.

- Motion Tracking Controller (Residual Reinforcement Learning): To faithfully execute the optimized trajectory under real-world disturbances, an asymmetric Actor-Critic residual RL framework is employed. The Actor observes noisy tracking errors and local obstacle distances to output small joint target offsets $\delta a_t$ relative to the nominal trajectory, which drive a PD controller. The Critic receives privileged information such as exact contact forces during training via PPO.

sections.heading: Confined space benchmarks exceeding NIST standards and experimental results
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on the Unitree G1 across three challenging environments exceeding US NIST emergency response standards, including obstructed openings and tilted stairs. While conventional baselines that omit knee trajectories completely failed in restricted openings, the proposed framework generated valid trajectories with high probability in just a few minutes. Furthermore, the residual RL policy achieved an over 95% traversal success rate under physics simulation disturbances.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted using a 27-DoF model of the human-scale Unitree G1 humanoid. Three test environments exceeding US NIST rescue standards were established: an Unobstructed Hole, an Obstructed Hole with protruding obstacles, and Tilted Stairs where the robot must brace against handrail walls with its palms. The confinement metric $C_r$, defined as the ratio of opening cross-sectional area to robot cross-sectional area, was set to $C_r = 1.4 \sim 1.5$—an extreme tightness requiring the robot to crouch and compress its profile to pass.

Key empirical findings include:

- Benchmark Success Rate and Compute Time: The proposed method achieved a 100% success rate across randomized initial positions in the Tilted Stairs and Unobstructed Hole, and reached a 65% success rate in the most challenging Obstructed Hole. Optimization times averaged 3 to 6 minutes even in the hardest setting (227 seconds excluding outliers), which is practical for long-horizon multi-contact planning.

- Comparison with Baselines: Comparisons were made against ROM-based spline-guided methods that omit knee paths, as well as naive linear interpolation. While baselines found solutions in the relatively spacious Tilted Stairs, they failed nearly 100% of the time (trapped in local minima, failing to converge) in Hole environments where lifting knees high over obstacles was required. This proves that explicitly guiding rigid-body volumes like knees, rather than just end-effectors, is vital.

- Ablation Studies: Omitting Stage 2 volume-informed SCA caused the success rate in the Obstructed Hole to plummet to just a single run. Additionally, skipping the first pass of Stage 3 (which aligns dynamics first) started the solver too close to hard bounds, inducing numerical instability and degrading reliability.

- Closed-Loop Simulation Tracking: Training the residual RL policy on the optimized trajectory converged rapidly in roughly 200 million environment steps (2000 iterations across 4096 parallel environments). Under physics simulation with friction variations, link mass randomizations, and continuous push disturbances, it exhibited high robustness, successfully clearing the openings over 95% of the time.

captions.F4: Dimensional comparison between the three challenging confined benchmark environments (left) and US NIST standard environments (right). The benchmark openings (Hole) are narrower than NIST hurdles, and the stairs (Tilted Stairs) feature a steep 55-degree incline requiring palm bracing.
captions.F5: Joint angle profiles (top) and minimum clearance distances (bottom) during traversal of the Obstructed Hole. Hip and knee joints operate right along the dashed joint limit lines, safely maintaining tight clearance margins of just millimeters to centimeters against environmental and self-collisions.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future work: hardware deployment and autonomous contact search
sections.summary: By performing differentiable collision detection over reachable rigid-body volumes, this three-stage planning framework accomplishes whole-body humanoid planning and robust RL tracking in previously intractable confined spaces. Future directions include physical hardware validation, integration with autonomous contact sequence discovery, and mobile manipulation while carrying bulky payloads in confined quarters.
sections.details:
This paper presented a novel whole-body planning (WBP) framework for humanoids navigating highly confined spaces. The core breakthrough lies in departing from simplified point-based guides and directly solving differentiable collision avoidance over reachability-constrained rigid-body volumes. This reliably steers full-order trajectory optimizers to feasible solutions even under tight confinement ratios of $C_r < 1.5$.

Moreover, the synthesized high-quality whole-body trajectories serve as effective references for training disturbance-resilient residual reinforcement learning policies.

The authors outline three key areas for future work:
- Real-world validation and deployment on the physical Unitree G1 hardware.
- Integrating the planning framework with efficient contact search pipelines to replace pre-specified contact sequences, building a fully autonomous confined-space navigation policy.
- Extending to loco-manipulation tasks that require transporting and manipulating large obstacles or cargo within confined spaces.

takeaways: In confined-space trajectory optimization, prior guidance via differentiable collision detection using proxy rigid bodies (capsules, spheres) rather than point approximations plays a decisive role in escaping local minima.
A two-pass optimization strategy that relaxes hard collision bounds first to reconcile nonlinear dynamics and torque limits dramatically improves numerical stability.

Even for extreme-posture whole-body motions where RL exploration fails from scratch, conducting residual RL using high-quality optimized trajectories as references enables rapid learning of robust policies.
limitations: Contact sequences (the ordering and surfaces for hand and foot placements) are assumed to be pre-specified, relying on separate modules for autonomous contact discovery.
Optimization compute time takes several minutes (averaging 2 to 6 minutes), making real-time replanning during dynamic environmental changes difficult at present.

Evaluation is confined to high-fidelity physics simulation (MuJoCo); hardware validation addressing real-world backlash, contact sensor noise, and communication delays on a physical humanoid remains unverified.
